job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In a recent industrial safety seminar, experts highlighted critical fire safety protocols. A major point of discussion was electrical fires, which are common in factories. Experts warned that using water on these fires is dangerous because water conducts electricity, potentially causing fatal shocks. Instead, carbon dioxide extinguishers are preferred as they cut off the oxygen supply without conducting current. The seminar also addressed the dangers of incomplete combustion in poorly ventilated rooms. When fuels like coal burn with insufficient oxygen, they produce carbon monoxide, a deadly, invisible gas that is far more dangerous than visible smoke. Furthermore, the experts debunked the myth that metals are inherently non-combustible. While many metals resist burning, fine powders of metals like magnesium can burn intensely, releasing significant heat. Regarding fuel selection, the speakers cautioned that a high calorific value is not the only factor for choosing a fuel. Factors like cost, availability, and safety are equally vital. Finally, they explained that spontaneous combustion is not a random event; it occurs when a substance reaches its ignition temperature through internal chemical reactions, often due to poor storage of oily rags. Understanding these principles is essential for preventing accidents in both homes and workplaces, ensuring that we handle fuels and fire hazards with the scientific caution they require.

items.evidence: Experts warned that using water on these fires is dangerous because water conducts electricity, potentially causing fatal shocks.
items.q: Why is pouring water on a factory wiring fire a bad idea?
options: The current can travel through the water to people
The water would make the fire spread wider
The water would remove oxygen too slowly
The water would damage the machines inside
items.explain: Water conducts electricity, so the current can pass through it and shock the person holding the water.

wrong.why: thinks water spreads all fires, a common everyday belief
thinks water works but is only slow
picks a nearby worry about machines, not the shock danger

items.evidence: When fuels like coal burn with insufficient oxygen, they produce carbon monoxide, a deadly, invisible gas that is far more dangerous than visible smoke.
items.q: A coal stove burns in a closed room with little air. What is the main danger?
options: A hidden poisonous gas builds up in the room
Only thick smoke fills the room, which is harmless
The coal burns hotter and the room overheats
The coal turns into a different fuel
items.explain: Coal burning with too little oxygen makes carbon monoxide, an invisible deadly gas, which is worse than smoke.

wrong.why: thinks incomplete combustion gives only smoke
thinks less oxygen gives a hotter fire
mixes up burning with a change of fuel type

items.evidence: While many metals resist burning, fine powders of metals like magnesium can burn intensely, releasing significant heat.
items.q: Which situation shows that a metal can catch fire?
options: Magnesium in fine powder form burning with heat
A solid iron rod melting in a furnace
A copper wire glowing when current passes
Aluminium foil becoming warm in sunlight
items.explain: Fine magnesium powder burns intensely and releases heat, so metals are not always non-combustible.

items.evidence: Regarding fuel selection, the speakers cautioned that a high calorific value is not the only factor for choosing a fuel.
items.q: Fuel X gives the most heat per kg but is costly and unsafe. What should a factory do?
options: Also weigh its cost, safety and availability
Choose it, since heat is all that matters
Choose it, since cost and safety never change
Reject every fuel that gives high heat
items.explain: High calorific value is not the only factor; cost, availability and safety are equally important when choosing a fuel.

wrong.why: thinks highest calorific value is always best
over-generalises the caution into a ban

items.evidence: Finally, they explained that spontaneous combustion is not a random event; it occurs when a substance reaches its ignition temperature through internal chemical reactions, often due to poor storage of oily rags.
items.q: A heap of oily rags suddenly catches fire in a shed. What best explains this?
options: Slow reactions inside heated it to ignition temperature
It happened by chance with no heat involved
Someone must have lit it with an outside flame
The shed air alone gave it enough heat
items.explain: Internal chemical reactions raised the rags to their ignition temperature, so the fire had a cause.

wrong.why: thinks spontaneous combustion has no cause
thinks every fire needs an outside flame
thinks surrounding air supplies the heat
